key: Like a dark steed adorned with pearl, the Fathers have decorated heaven With constellations. They set the light in day, in night the darkness. Brhaspati cleft the rock and found the cattle.
s: Near the close of a hymn on Bṛhaspati winning the cows from Vala, the singer looks to the night sky; Sāyaṇa, on 10.68.11, reads ‘the Fathers’ as the guarding gods, who lit heaven with the lunar mansions when Bṛhaspati broke the rock.

evidence.gloss: The Fathers, the gods who protect, lit up heaven, the sky world, all around with the lunar mansions, Aśvinī and the rest (the root piś, ‘to form’, here means ‘to light’). The comparison: as men adorn a dark-coloured horse with golden ornaments, so did they. So too they set darkness in the night, and in the day the light called the sun (grammatical note on the accent). When Bṛhaspati broke the rock, the mass of stone that Vala held, and, having broken it, found the cows that stood there: then the gods did thus. That is the sense.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref 10.68.11, at [904,11]). Sāyaṇa on 10.68.11 glosses pitaraḥ as pālayitāro devāḥ (the protecting gods), nakṣatrebhiḥ as Aśvinī and the rest (the lunar mansions), apiṃśan as abhito ’dīpayan (lit up all around), and ties the deed in time to Bṛhaspati’s breaking of the rock (yadā … tadā devā evam akārṣuḥ). The sentence carries this without drift. Plain sense: 10.68 is to Bṛhaspati winning the cows from Vala, and 10.68.11 is the second-last stanza, on heaven decked with constellations; faithful.
